topic:
Research question: Will the periodic table ever be complete?
Context: The periodic table currently consists of 118 elements, the last four of which were announced in 2016. The International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC), which formally verifies, recognizes, and names new elements, has a challenging task. Its guidelines for the criteria for element discovery were established 29 years ago, yet in 2018, IUPAC issued an update illustrating the challenges associated with resolving whether the periodic table will ever be complete. IUPAC’s updated report addressed how previously utilized methods and technologies for discovering new elements were being supplanted by innovative approaches. As new techniques are developed, it is possible more elements will be found—the limitations of human inventiveness may be our only obstacle.

ideas.title: Verification First-Passage Assay for the Verifiable Completion Boundary of the Periodic Table
ideas.motivation: The question whether the periodic table can ever be complete is not only a synthesis problem; it is also a verification problem because IUPAC/IUPAP recognition depends on evidence that can become extremely difficult to obtain for few short-lived atoms [Author et al., 2020](https://openalex.org/W3048546628). Hot-fusion reaction surveys identify plausible projectile-target routes toward elements beyond Z = 118 and predict potentially accessible evaporation-residue cross sections, but entrance-channel effects, quasifission, and survival probabilities remain major obstacles [Author et al., 2020](https://openalex.org/W3111464399). Theoretical predictions for superheavy stability must extrapolate nuclear interactions into sparsely constrained regions, so lifetimes and fission barriers are uncertain [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4415525127). At the same time, chemical identification beyond the heaviest studied elements is a single-atom thermalization and transport challenge [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4412961862). The field therefore lacks a quantitative estimand that separates a physical nuclear-existence limit from a verification limit. This proposal imports single-entity residence-time analysis from single-molecule separation science [Author et al., 2020](https://openalex.org/W3087606226) and uncertainty-quantified reaction-network inference from Bayesian scientific machine learning [Author et al., 2024](https://openalex.org/W4392592391) to create a testable verification first-passage assay for superheavy-element discovery.
ideas.methods:
1. Verification first-passage estimand: We define a latent state x = (Z, A, reaction channel) and event-level observables including decay-chain graph, decay energies/times, optional characteristic X-rays, and time-stamped transport/arrival data under a controlled intervention u. The verification first-passage time tau_v is the earliest time at which the posterior Bayes factor for one Z against the best competing Z exceeds a pre-registered threshold; the minimum verification capability C_min is the smallest expected production-detection budget required to reach that threshold with a specified probability. Non-stationary nuisance variables such as temperature drift, surface aging, charge-state changes, and detector dead time are included in the likelihood, making the estimand identifiable from coupled decay and residence-time data. This turns IUPAC-style discovery evidence into a quantitative, comparable boundary measure [Author et al., 2020](https://openalex.org/W3048546628), and it uses first-passage statistics appropriate to rare single atoms in buffer-gas/transport systems [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4412961862) [Author et al., 2020](https://openalex.org/W3087606226).
2. Active modulated transport discriminator: The transport stage is made into an active mechanistic discriminator by adding repeatable, structured modulation to a buffer-gas/atmospheric-pressure transfer line, for example segmented temperature zones, switchable surface chemistries, or periodic electric-field/gas-composition pulses, building on simulated superheavy gas-flow devices [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4412961862). Atoms with different adsorption enthalpies, diffusion coefficients, or charge-state equilibria then produce distinct residence-time and breakthrough distributions. The controlled quantity is the intervention-induced change in mutual information between residence-time/first-passage observables and atomic-number-relevant chemical identity. The modulation pattern is the controlled factor; mean flow, pressure, mean temperature, geometry, and detection window are held fixed so that any increase in information can be attributed to structured element-specific first-passage behavior, as in single-entity separation analysis [Author et al., 2020](https://openalex.org/W3087606226).
3. Bayesian single-event digital twin: The inference engine is a Bayesian single-event digital twin adapted from uncertainty-quantified reaction-network discovery [Author et al., 2024](https://openalex.org/W4392592391). It represents the full pipeline as a stochastic network: entrance-channel capture, compound-nucleus formation, quasifission loss, evaporation-residue survival, decay, thermalization, transport, and detection. Production priors are constrained by hot-fusion reaction surveys and entrance-channel effects [Author et al., 2020](https://openalex.org/W3111464399), while nuclear-stability and decay priors include model uncertainty from superheavy-interaction extrapolation [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4415525127). The model outputs posterior probabilities for Z/A, tau_v, C_min, and the probability of meeting the verification threshold under a given experimental configuration.
4. Completion-boundary decision assay: The completion-boundary assay uses the calibrated digital twin to evaluate candidate reactions and isotopes for Z > 118. If predicted nuclear existence probability, lifetime, or cross section falls below the verification requirement even under optimal transport, the candidate is classified as physically limited; if the nucleus could exist long enough but C_min exceeds plausible beam time, efficiency, or chemistry performance, it is verification limited. It also ranks calibration and beam-time actions by expected reduction in C_min or expected information gain. This directly addresses the periodic-table completion question by distinguishing nuclear-stability boundaries from experimental-verification boundaries under IUPAC-relevant evidence standards [Author et al., 2020](https://openalex.org/W3048546628) and current synthesis predictions [Author et al., 2020](https://openalex.org/W3111464399) [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4415525127).
Analogy — borrows single-entity trajectory/residence-time analysis and stochastic separation modeling from Transforming Separation Science with Single-Molecule Methods; adapted as each superheavy recoil is treated as a single entity; controlled gas-flow modulation turns residence-time/first-passage distributions into an atomic-number-relevant observable for verification [Author et al., 2020](https://openalex.org/W3087606226)
Analogy — borrows Bayesian uncertainty-quantified reaction-network digital twin inferred from sparse time-resolved events from Uncertainty quantified discovery of chemical reaction systems via Bayesian scientific machine learning; adapted as the superheavy pipeline of fusion, quasifission, survival, decay, transport, and detection is modeled as a Bayesian network with posteriors over latent Z/A and nuisance parameters, yielding verification first-passage estimates [Author et al., 2024](https://openalex.org/W4392592391)
Experiment plan: Phase 0: Build or simulate a bench-scale buffer-gas/atmospheric-pressure transfer line with interchangeable wall chemistries and independently controlled temperature or field modulation; calibrate flow, pressure, baseline residence time, and detector timing using stable aerosols or long-lived radiotracers.; Pre-register the primary hypothesis and success metrics: structured modulation must increase mutual information between observations and species/atomic-number-relevant identity and reduce the expected number of atoms needed to reach the Bayes-factor threshold, relative to passive and randomized controls.; Select a fixed chemically active wall condition and a fixed test set of available heavy radionuclide or homolog species with distinct adsorption/charge behavior; keep injection rate, geometry, gas composition, pressure, mean temperature, mean residence time, detector settings, and analysis thresholds fixed.; Primary one-factor experiment: vary only the modulation pattern among passive transport, structured periodic modulation, and amplitude-matched randomized modulation, using single-species and fixed two-species mixture runs; record injection time, first-passage/arrival time, decay time, decay energy, and any correlated X-ray or gamma events.; Controls: chemically active wall without modulation (chemistry alone), inert wall with structured modulation (modulation alone), passive inert transport (neither), decay-only bypass, randomized modulation, blank background runs, and an unstructured late-fusion model that combines empirical transport and decay histograms without mechanistic coupling.; Confounder exclusion: measure decay losses during transport with known half-lives; perform surface mass-balance and desorption assays to rule out memory effects; use computational-fluid-dynamics tracer tests to rule out turbulence or dead-volume artifacts; monitor charge-state distributions; and verify detector dead time and timing jitter with pulsed sources.; Analyze the primary phase with the Bayesian single-event model to estimate residence-time likelihoods, posterior species/group assignments, mutual information, tau_v, and C_min; attribute any improvement specifically to structured modulation if randomized modulation and component-alone controls do not reproduce it.; Only after the core hypothesis is confirmed, vary secondary parameters one at a time: modulation amplitude, frequency, surface chemistry, gas pressure, temperature gradient, and transport length, while retaining the same primary information metric.; Calibrate the superheavy extrapolation using hot-fusion reaction priors and ensembles of nuclear-stability models; propagate uncertainty in cross sections, lifetimes, fission barriers, and transport times to tau_v and C_min for candidate Z = 119, 120, and heavier systems.; Produce completion-boundary maps that classify candidate isotopes/reactions as physically limited, verification limited, or verifiable under near-future capabilities, and output pre-registered recommendations for the reaction/modulation/chemistry combination that minimizes C_min.
ideas.method_overview: This method is intended to solve the absence of an experimentally anchored completion-boundary test for superheavy elements; it can be divided into 4 parts: (1) a verification first-passage time and minimum verification capability estimand, (2) an active modulated gas-flow transport discriminator, (3) a Bayesian single-event digital twin linking synthesis, survival, decay, transport, and detection, and (4) a decision assay that classifies candidate elements as physically limited or verification limited. The primary hypothesis is that structured modulation of transport/adsorption conditions causally increases the mutual information between single-atom observations and atomic-number-relevant chemical identity, relative to passive transport and decay-only evidence, while mean residence time and detection efficiency are held fixed.

experiment_plan: Phase 0: Build or simulate a bench-scale buffer-gas/atmospheric-pressure transfer line with interchangeable wall chemistries and independently controlled temperature or field modulation; calibrate flow, pressure, baseline residence time, and detector timing using stable aerosols or long-lived radiotracers.

Pre-register the primary hypothesis and success metrics: structured modulation must increase mutual information between observations and species/atomic-number-relevant identity and reduce the expected number of atoms needed to reach the Bayes-factor threshold, relative to passive and randomized controls.

Select a fixed chemically active wall condition and a fixed test set of available heavy radionuclide or homolog species with distinct adsorption/charge behavior; keep injection rate, geometry, gas composition, pressure, mean temperature, mean residence time, detector settings, and analysis thresholds fixed.

Primary one-factor experiment: vary only the modulation pattern among passive transport, structured periodic modulation, and amplitude-matched randomized modulation, using single-species and fixed two-species mixture runs; record injection time, first-passage/arrival time, decay time, decay energy, and any correlated X-ray or gamma events.

Controls: chemically active wall without modulation (chemistry alone), inert wall with structured modulation (modulation alone), passive inert transport (neither), decay-only bypass, randomized modulation, blank background runs, and an unstructured late-fusion model that combines empirical transport and decay histograms without mechanistic coupling.

Confounder exclusion: measure decay losses during transport with known half-lives; perform surface mass-balance and desorption assays to rule out memory effects; use computational-fluid-dynamics tracer tests to rule out turbulence or dead-volume artifacts; monitor charge-state distributions; and verify detector dead time and timing jitter with pulsed sources.

Analyze the primary phase with the Bayesian single-event model to estimate residence-time likelihoods, posterior species/group assignments, mutual information, tau_v, and C_min; attribute any improvement specifically to structured modulation if randomized modulation and component-alone controls do not reproduce it.

Only after the core hypothesis is confirmed, vary secondary parameters one at a time: modulation amplitude, frequency, surface chemistry, gas pressure, temperature gradient, and transport length, while retaining the same primary information metric.

Calibrate the superheavy extrapolation using hot-fusion reaction priors and ensembles of nuclear-stability models; propagate uncertainty in cross sections, lifetimes, fission barriers, and transport times to tau_v and C_min for candidate Z = 119, 120, and heavier systems.

Produce completion-boundary maps that classify candidate isotopes/reactions as physically limited, verification limited, or verifiable under near-future capabilities, and output pre-registered recommendations for the reaction/modulation/chemistry combination that minimizes C_min.

ideas.novelty_justification: The closest existing combination is the IUPAC/IUPAP discovery criteria plus the UniCell/atmospheric-pressure gas-flow simulation study, with hot-fusion entrance-channel surveys and superheavy stability calculations supplying production and nuclear priors. Those references already connect superheavy synthesis, decay-chain verification, and gas-phase transport/chemistry. The proposal adds a formal verification first-passage estimand, a minimum verification capability metric, active modulation of transport to increase mutual information, and a Bayesian digital twin coupling the full pipeline. This is more than a trivial recombination because the modulation-based first-passage assay is a testable mechanism. However, the novelty is still largely combinatorial: residence-time/thermochromatographic identification, decay-chain evidence, reaction priors, and uncertainty quantification are known ingredients, and the Bayesian/single-entity framing is imported rather than a new superheavy-specific physical mechanism. Thus the idea is novel relative to the references but not high.
improvement_suggestions: Sharpen the mechanistic claim by making decay itself perturb transport, for example using alpha decay, fission fragments, recoil charge-state changes, or decay-induced desorption to create decay-gated residence-time signatures that are intrinsic to superheavy atoms rather than generic externally imposed modulation.

Introduce a conceptual verification-boundary criterion, such as a provable identifiability or verification horizon, that specifies when no admissible modulation, chemistry, or beam-time budget can reach the required Bayes factor because of overlapping adsorption enthalpies, short half-lives, and background; then design adaptive modulation to approach that bound.
